initial_presentation: Patient 4 is a 34-year-old Turkish woman who has experienced arm and leg weakness and muscle atrophy since she was 15 years old. There is no family history of neuromuscular disease, and her 5 siblings do not exhibit any symptoms. She has been taking riluzole since she was 15 years old. Her symptoms have shown slow progression over time. During her most recent evaluation at age 34, she was using a wheelchair but could walk short distances with assistance. She did not have difficulty swallowing and did not need oxygen supplementation. Her weight was within normal limits.

The fourth child in the family, a girl, was born at term to a 28-year-old mother and a 32-year-old father. At birth, her length was 53 cm (+0.7 SD) and her weight was 4000 g (+1.3 SD). Early developmental concerns included recurrent constipation, a noticeable urine odor, growth delays, and developmental delays. She began walking independently at 2.5 years, albeit with some stepping issues, and started speaking more clearly by age 3. Around age 3, she experienced recurrent fractures following minor traumas, which were managed with casts and pins.

An 18-year-old female patient presented with bleeding gums and swelling on the right side of the lower jaw for 6 months. The swelling, initially the size of a peanut, grew slowly to its current size. There was no associated pain. The patient also reported progressive hearing loss over 2 years and a history of multiple bone fractures, up to thirty, occurring spontaneously from minor injuries since childhood. Medical and family histories were noncontributory. Clinical examination revealed a short, stout appearance with bowing of the upper and lower limbs. Extraoral examination showed unilateral facial asymmetry. Intraorally, a bony prominence of the mandible extending from tooth 43 to the mesial aspect of tooth 47, measuring approximately 2 cm × 1 cm, was observed. The swelling was well-circumscribed, nontender, and hard in consistency, with slightly erythematous mucosa over it. Lymph nodes were not palpable.

A 62-year-old woman was admitted to the Emergency Department due to a painful and rapidly enlarging mass on the left back area. She had a medical history of surgery and skin grafting for a large hematoma on the right back area 30 years prior. Initial physical examination in the ED showed vital signs with a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 120 beats/min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and an axillary temperature of 36.5℃. A soft mass measuring 10×5×3 cm with tenderness on palpation was noted on the left back area. The mass was scarlet-colored, non-pulsating, and had a well-demarcated border. Multiple areas of hyperpigmentation (café-au-lait spots) were observed on her torso and extremities, along with axillary freckling. Routine blood samples taken on admission showed a white blood cell count of 11,400/µL, hemoglobin concentration of 12.

A 42-year-old male with no history of exposure to industrial toxins or radioactive substances was admitted in November 2018. He presented with ecchymosis on the left lower limb persisting for over a month, gingival bleeding, and fatigue for 10 days, which had worsened over the past 2 days. Physical examination revealed anemia, scattered mucosal and skin bleeding spots, normal heart rhythm, clear lung sounds, a soft abdomen, no palpable liver or spleen below the ribs, and no lower limb edema. Initial blood chemistry results showed a white blood cell count of 8.

A 16-year-old female presented with tingling pain in her left leg and continuous involuntary movements of her left great toe one month following a second untethering surgery. The movements, characterized by extension and flexion of the great toe, occurred during wakefulness and early sleep stages and could not be voluntarily controlled. The pain was not aggravated by walking, sitting, or straining. At birth, she had a sacral dimple at the S2–3 vertebral level. Four years prior, she experienced voiding difficulty and underwent untethering surgery to address a lipomeningomyelocele at the S2 level of the conus medullaris.

A 25-year-old male presented with a primary concern of teeth misalignment since childhood. The patient also reported experiencing hearing difficulties in the left ear from a young age. Extra-oral examination revealed a transverse cleft at the right angle of the mouth, preauricular tissue tags, and incompetent lips. There was noticeable bilateral facial asymmetry and macrostomia, with an inter-incisal distance of 43 mm. Intraoral examination showed missing teeth 16 and 47, spacing between teeth 11, 12, 13, 14, 42, 43, and 44, proclined teeth 11, 12, 13, and 43, a crossbite involving teeth 24 and 34, increased overjet, and a high arched palate.

A 40-year-old female patient presented with a noticeable change in the shape of the pupil in her left eye, without other eye-related complaints. She wears glasses and has no other systemic conditions.

Patient 6 is a white male who reported experiencing reduced night and peripheral vision starting at approximately 25 years old. He has no family history of similar symptoms. His medical history includes hearing loss in adulthood, which necessitated the use of hearing aids, and peripheral neuropathy, leading to decreased sensitivity in distal regions and ataxia. Although he did not personally notice any issues with his sense of smell, his wife observed that he often fails to detect odors in their home.

A 45-year-old female patient reported experiencing pain in the left molar region of the lower jaw for the past month. The patient was in good overall health, and her physical examination did not reveal any notable abnormalities. An intraoral examination identified a decayed left mandibular first permanent molar and the absence of the second permanent molar, which had been extracted 2 years prior due to decay.
